The answer [in a graph](https://i.sli.mg/gpIblv.gif).

Worker productivity worldwide has been skyrocketing. In 1950 if it took 50 people to produce the goods for 100 people, those same 50 people can now a days produce the goods for 600 people! There are more industries today than in the 50s but not enough to sustain meaningful employment, particularly as productivity continues to see rapid increases.

This is also the reason even though you now earn vastly more money for your company than any point in history, you're earning about the same wage that your parents or grandparents in the 70s did. When companies don't need as many workers they're under no obligation to compete on salary. It's the reason you see huge numbers of people even with 'real' degrees underemployed or even unemployed. It's not that we're vastly more educated as some have speculated. In the 70s we peaked at about 24% of people having a 4 year degree. Today that number is 34%.

Think about the next 30 years and where we're going. How do you see worker productivity changing?

Automation will bring this to a climax. Automation will see rapid increases in productivity and associated increases in unemployment which is going to result in an inevitable transition towards a new economic system. Even the central bank is preparing for this. [Here](https://research.stlouisfed.org/wp/more/2014-047/?utm_reader=feedly) is a 2014 from one of the Federal Reserve banks. The first sentence of that abstract tells it all:

> **Universal Basic Income versus Unemployment Insurance** : In this paper we compare the welfare effects of unemployment insurance (UI) with an universal basic income (UBI) system in an economy with idiosyncratic shocks to employment.

This isn't some distant future 10 or 20 years down the line type thing. We'll likely see the first private fully autonomous vehicles on the streets before 2020. Uber's CEO has stated he himself would like to purchase the entire first line of Tesla's self driving vehicles, estimated at 500,000. Great for him, but not so great for the 500,000 people who could've been driving those cabs. This isn't a bad thing either, it's actually a great thing. It means those 500,000 need not live a life of simply driving people from point A to point B, but it's going to require a fundamental shift in our economic system.
